Row 79 and the cemetery work of 30 September are the same lesson in miniature: the map looked empty at Senj because the data was filtered, not because the ground was bare.

**FOLLOWED UP THE SAME DAY, AND THE ANSWER IS ONE COUNTRY.** «Survey the 329» is not a diffuse backlog. It is concentrated: **France 200, Germany 32, Bulgaria 30**, and everything else in single figures. France alone is 61% of every unsurveyed provider this atlas holds.

Set beside Italy it is embarrassing, and it is the clearest instruction this worklist has ever contained:

| | providers | unsurveyed | places | volumes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Italy | 129 | **2** | 2,897 | **1,343,253** |
| France | **205** | **200** | 81 | **1,513** |
| Germany | 37 | 32 | 191 | 4,218 |
| Bulgaria | 30 | 30 | 0 | 0 |

**FRANCE HAS MORE ARCHIVES CATALOGUED THAN ITALY AND A THOUSANDTH OF THE VOLUMES.** 203 of its 205 are regional — the archives départementales and communales, which are the free, online, état-civil and parish-register backbone of French genealogy and among the most generous public record holdings in Europe. Nothing about France is harder than Italy. The only difference in this atlas is that somebody surveyed Italy's 129 and nobody has opened France's 200.

Bulgaria's 30 are not even triaged — `triage: null` on every one, all state archives, so nobody has so much as looked at whether they answer.

So the order narrows: **France first**, then Germany's 32, then Bulgaria's 30 — before any further breadth anywhere. And note what this does NOT need: no new region, no gazetteer work, no licence question. The addresses are already in providers.json and have been all along.

**9 OCTOBER: THE ARCHIVE COUNT IS NO LONGER MOSTLY UNOPENED.** This row measured **329 of 547 providers unsurveyed, 60%**. It is now **117 of 555, 21.1%** — and 62 of those 117 carry a recorded reason, so only **55 have never been looked at**.

France was the answer, and then two more countries were: **Bulgaria's 30 and Germany's 31 both collapse to a handful of institutions.** Bulgaria's 28 state archives are branches of one agency on one site — one survey, 30 free rows, and the national library turned out to hold freely digitised **defteri and sidjili**, the Ottoman population and court registers, which is a better door than the archives for anything before 1893. Germany's 31 are really about twelve portals: Niedersachsen's five share Arcinsys with Bremen and with the Kreis, Stadt, church and university archives; Baden-Württemberg's six share Online-Findmittel.

**THE LESSON FOR THE REMAINING 55 IS COUNT THE INSTITUTIONS, NOT THE ROWS.** France cost two long rows because its 108 communes were 108 separate websites. Bulgaria cost an afternoon because its 30 archives were one. Before surveying a country, group its rows by host: the ratio of hosts to rows predicts the work almost exactly.

What is left is a long tail — **FR 42 (all with reasons), BR 6, HR 5, CZ 4, JP 3, PH 3**, then ones and twos. No country is worth a row of its own any more.

rows.what: Survey France's 95 departmental archives — the half of the backlog that holds the records
rows.note:
Row 80 said France was 200 unsurveyed providers and 61% of the whole backlog. Looked at properly, that is **two different populations filed together**:

- **108 `ac-` rows — archives COMMUNALES.** A commune's own municipal papers. Thin online, and mostly not where registers live.
- **95 `ad-` rows — archives DÉPARTEMENTALES.** One per department, and these are the ones that matter: French departmental archives put état civil and registres paroissiaux online, free, for most of the country. **Two were surveyed** — Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin.

Surveying France alphabetically would therefore spend most of the effort on the wrong half. Do the 95 first.

**A LIVENESS SWEEP OF ALL 95, 5 October: 85 answered a scripted request, 10 refused.** The refusals are the interesting part, and they are NOT link rot:

| code | count | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| 403 | 3 | Forbidden to a script |
| 418 | 2 | the teapot code sites use to turn scripts away |
| 404 | 2 | the only ones likely to be genuinely wrong addresses |
| 000 | 3 | no connection completed |

**ad-tarn answered 418 and is perfectly alive**: in a browser it resolves to the real Archives Départementales du Tarn, with an anti-DDoS flood page standing in front of scripts. It has since been surveyed and promoted to `free` — «consultation en ligne de documents numérisés», no account. So a refusal from a sweep is a gate, not a grave, and every one of those nine rows now says so in its triageNote rather than being written off.

WHAT IS LEFT is the slow part and there is no shortcut: each departmental portal is bespoke software, so there is no pattern to match and no bulk promotion to be had. 93 of the 95 still need a browser, one at a time. Alsace CEA and Mayotte need a corrected URL first.

---

**9 October: ten surveyed in one sitting, 80 left.** All ten free, none asking for an account to reach the registers. What each one says about itself is now in its `what`, because the access class is the least interesting thing a survey finds:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Calvados** | its 4E description records that the registers were «microfilmage par les Mormons» in the 1960s and that THAT microfilm is what was digitised, «complété pour la période postérieure à 1860» — the 1860 line, stated by the archive that drew it |
| **Charente-Maritime** | «Plus de 5,5 millions d'images consultables depuis chez vous», and separately the PROTESTANT registers 1561–1793 and 1806–1831 |
| **Bouches-du-Rhône** | parish and civil registers XVIe s.–1925, and notarial répertoires running from **1361** |
| **Côtes-d'Armor** | ~5 million views, and the rare admission that «des pages ont malheureusement été omises lors des opérations de numérisation» — written into `what`, because a blank there is not evidence the register is blank |
| **Cantal** | «état civil des origines jusqu'en 1932 (années 1950 pour les décès)» |
| **Creuse** | XVIe siècle to 1922; births and marriages stop December 1920, which is the privacy window and not a gap |
| Corrèze · Côte-d'Or · Rhône · Charente | all free, all with the register search open |

**CHARENTE IS THE ONE WITH A SHAPE WORTH KNOWING.** Two tiers, divided by the hundred-year rule: «les tables décennales ne comportant pas de données à caractère personnel, elles sont visibles par tous, sans restriction ! Les actes d'état civil ne sont diffusables sur Internet qu'une fois un délai de 100 ans passé» — for those you sign in with **FranceConnect**, the French state identity service. Classed `free`, not `account`, because the login is only for the most recent century, which is closed on paper too; and not `mixed`, because nothing here is paid.

**AND A SECOND BOT GATE, CONFIRMING ad-tarn WAS NOT A ONE-OFF.** `lasource.archives.lacharente.fr` answers a browser only after a «Making sure you're not a bot!» interstitial. A refusal from a scripted sweep is a gate, not a grave — twice over now.

**WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED:** no individual register image was opened on any of the ten. The bar is the one ad-tarn was promoted on — catalogue and register search reachable with no account asked anywhere — and ad-calvados says so in its own triageNote.

**THE RATE.** Calvados took about fifteen browser calls, its catalogue being JavaScript and its commune list behind a select widget. The other nine took one to three each, once the shape was clear: home page, find the «archives numérisées» or «archives en ligne» link, read that one page — and where the page is server-rendered, fetch it from the page context without navigating at all.

**Same day, seven more: 21 of 95 free, 74 left, and one genuinely shut.**

**ALPES-MARITIMES IS THE FIRST REAL REFUSAL.** `www.archives06.fr` answers a real browser — not a script — with «The requested URL was rejected. Please consult with your administrator.» and a support ID. That is a web application firewall declining the connection outright, not an anti-DDoS page a browser walks through. Left `unsurveyed` and written down rather than worked around; it wants a human on an ordinary connection, or a letter to the archive.

**CHER is the one with the research caveat.** The greffe collection of parish registers before 1792 is digitised in full, but «la collection communale, souvent plus ancienne, n'a été numérisée que pour les communes ayant procédé à un dépôt» — so the older series is largely NOT online, and its absence from this site says nothing about whether the register survives. Diffusion is 100 years for births and 75 for marriages; the most recent acts online are 1947.

Also free: **Alpes-de-Haute-Provence**, **Dordogne**, **Drôme**, **Eure-et-Loir** (which also holds the Voves internment camp files), and **Finistère**, whose état civil search faceted by commune and act type runs with no account at all.

**A THIRD BOT GATE.** `recherche.archives.finistere.fr` also answers only after «Making sure you're not a bot!». With ad-tarn and ad-charente that is three, and the pattern is now established well enough to say it plainly: **a scripted sweep's refusal predicts nothing about whether an archive is open.** The 5 October liveness sweep's ten refusals should all be re-tried in a browser before any of them is believed.

**Still 9 October: 25 of 95 free, 70 to go, two shut.**

**GUADELOUPE is not a mainland département and its holdings say so.** 46,371 archive records open with no account, and its thematic collections are **esclavage** and **BUMIDOM** — the state scheme that moved Antilleans to mainland France from 1963 — alongside oral testimonies and the Algerian war. Anyone tracing a Guadeloupean family through the twentieth century is tracing it through BUMIDOM, and this is where that paper is.

**GERS is the second genuine refusal:** `www.archives32.fr` answers a real browser with «Attack detected» and serves nothing. With Alpes-Maritimes that is two firewalls declining outright — a different thing from the five «Making sure you're not a bot!» hosts, which a browser walks straight through.

Also free: **Gard** (and it holds the records of refugees from the Spanish Civil War), **Gironde** — «Registres paroissiaux et d'état civil (1538-1935)», plus *passeports pour l'étranger*, which is where a Bordelais emigration appears once the registers stop — and **Haute-Garonne**, whose date picker takes the **calendrier républicain**, Vendémiaire onward, because that is what the registers of 1793–1805 are actually dated in.

**THE TALLY OF GATES SO FAR:** five hosts answer a browser only after an anti-bot interstitial (tarn, charente, finistère, gironde, haute-garonne) and all five are open archives. Two refuse a browser outright (alpes-maritimes, gers). The first group would have been written off entirely by a scripted sweep, which is seven in twenty-nine surveyed — a quarter of the backlog misjudged if the sweep is believed.

**28 of 95, 67 to go.** Three more, and two of them change what the row is worth:

**HAUTE-SAVOIE IS ANOTHER STATE'S PAPER.** Savoy was Sardinian until 1860, and the digitised list says so: beside the état civil sit the **Mappes Sardes**, the **Tabellion d'Ancien Régime (1660–1798)** and the **Tabellion de la Restauration Sarde (1814–1861)**, with the comptes de châtellenie behind them. A researcher expecting only French series here will miss most of it. That is the jurisdiction trap this atlas documents for Istria and Alsace, in a third place.

**HAUTE-LOIRE STATES ITS REUSE TERMS, WHICH ALMOST NONE OF THEM DO.** «La réutilisation des informations publiques conservées par les Archives de la Haute-Loire est libre et gratuite, quelle que soit la finalité poursuivie… aucune autorisation du service d'archives n'est nécessaire.» Free, for any purpose, no permission. Worth recording as a licence and not just an access class, since this atlas has to tell a reuser what they are taking.

**HAUTE-MARNE has both collections online** and names them: collection départementale (1 E, 1566–1942, by commune — the duplicates kept since the Ancien Régime) and collection communale (E dépôt). Where Cher has only the greffe half digitised, Haute-Marne has both, and the difference is exactly what decides whether a missing register is missing or merely elsewhere.

**AN AUDIT PROMPTED FROM OUTSIDE, AND IT FOUND SOMETHING.** The session working the D'Arcy family took the note above about scripted refusals, re-tested its own four «blocked» verdicts, and one was simply wrong — BillionGraves answers a browser at once; the 403 and 400 that condemned it were facts about the request. Its conclusion is worth more than the correction:

> Four of my five coverage verdicts describe the SOURCE: covers it, partly, holds nothing, cannot answer. «Blocked» describes the ATTEMPT, and nothing in the row recorded which attempt or by what means. It is also the only one that feels like diligence — it says the archive tried and was refused, which closes the question and invites nobody to reopen it.

**THE SAME FAULT WAS HERE, IN 22 ROWS.** Ten `ac-` and twelve `ad-` providers carried the note «the homepage renders client-side; see scripts/render-pages.mjs» — undated, with no record of what was tried. What happened was a scripted fetch returning no usable content, and «renders client-side» was the explanation *assumed* for it. Three different things produce that empty body and nothing distinguished them: a site that genuinely needs JavaScript; an anti-bot interstitial, of which this survey has met **eight, every one fronting a free and open archive**; and a firewall refusing outright, of which it has met two, both genuinely shut.

**PROVED MIXED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** `ad-l-allier` carried that exact note. A browser gets its home page at once — 62 links, «Archives numérisées» in the navigation — and it is now surveyed and **free**, holding the Cahiers citoyens and the Grand Débat national of 2019 beside the registers. The other 21 notes now say what was actually tried, when, and that a browser has not been pointed at them yet.

32 of 95 free, 63 to go.

**FIVE OF THE TWELVE «renders client-side» ROWS OPENED, AND ALL FIVE WERE FREE.** 37 of 95 now. None of the twelve needed a renderer; they needed somebody to look.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Loiret** | registers to 1902, and over them **435,911 volunteer annotations** with 172,051 bookmarks and their own search — a name index on top of the images, which is the difference between browsing by commune and date and searching for the person you want |
| **Hautes-Pyrénées** | indexed by what a life does — «Naître, vivre et mourir» — including *registres de passeports* and the **cartes d'identité de Français (1943-1944)** |
| **Lot** | 17th century to 1922, and like Haute-Loire it states reuse: «la réutilisation de ces images est également libre et gratuite» |
| **Aube** | recensements now to 1975, **and it says what is missing from them**: «les listes de nombreuses communes sont absentes» for 1946 through 1975 |
| **Indre** | état civil, recensements, matricules, contrôle des actes, enregistrement |

**TWO ARCHIVES IN THIRTY-SEVEN STATE THEIR REUSE TERMS** — Haute-Loire and Lot, both saying free for any purpose with no permission needed. That is worth tracking separately from the access class: `free` says a reader may look, and it does not say an atlas may republish.

And Aube joins Cher and Côtes-d'Armor in the small group that documents its own gaps. Three in thirty-seven volunteer the thing that protects a researcher from reading absence as evidence.

**40 of 95. MANCHE ANSWERS THE ABSENCE QUESTION BETTER THAN ANY ARCHIVE HERE.**

Everything surviving up to 1892 is microfilmed and online. And if the act is not there, it tells you why:

> «Si vous ne trouvez pas l'acte que vous recherchez, c'est sans doute que le registre a été perdu avant son arrivée aux archives ou **détruit lors des bombardements en 1944**. On trouvera dans l'inventaire de la sous-série 2 E, **publié en 1943**, le détail des registres paroissiaux disparus.»

An inventory published the year *before* the bombing, listing what was already lost. So in the Manche a researcher can tell a 1944 loss from an older one — absence with a documented cause and a finding aid for it, which is the strongest form of the thing Cher, Côtes-d'Armor and Aube each gave a weaker version of.

**VENDÉE is the biggest index met so far**: over six million images, and the «Noms de Vendée» base of **3.5 million nominative records** over the top — larger than Loiret's 435,911 annotations. **Sarthe** keeps pre-1902 and post-1902 as separate collections with complete matricules.

**AND ONE OF THE TWELVE NOTES WAS TECHNICALLY RIGHT.** Vendée really does render client-side; a fetch of its pages returns nothing. That was never a reason to leave it unsurveyed — it is free and enormous — and it is the cleanest illustration of the fault: the note was not wrong about the mechanism, it was wrong to be an ending. Eight of the twelve are now surveyed and every one is free.

**ALL TWELVE «renders client-side» DÉPARTEMENTALES ARE NOW SURVEYED, AND ALL TWELVE ARE FREE.** Not one needed a renderer to be classified; one — Vendée — genuinely renders client-side and is six million images of free archive behind it. **44 of 95.** The ten remaining rows with that note are all `ac-` communales.

**YVELINES IS A JURISDICTION TRAP AND NOBODY WOULD GUESS IT.** It holds the registers of «une partie de l'ancienne **Seine-et-Oise**» — the département abolished in 1968 and split into six. A commune now in the Essonne, the Val-d'Oise or the Hauts-de-Seine may have its pre-1968 registers at Montigny-le-Bretonneux. 1.6 million views: parish registers 1533–1792, births 1792–1920, marriages 1792–1943, deaths into the 1950s for some communes. With Savoy's Sardinian tabellion and Alsace's German decades, that is the third French jurisdiction trap this survey has turned up, and the only one caused by a boundary change inside living memory.

**VAL-DE-MARNE states the communicability tiers more exactly than anyone else**: everything 1549–1922 online; some marriages and deaths to 1937 by commune; births and marriages 1923–1943 and deaths to 1952 in the reading room only; the greffe collection ends at 1952 and after that it is the mairies. Anybody writing a general rule about French privacy windows should read that row first — the rule is not one number.

**SAÔNE-ET-LOIRE**: «des millions de données accessibles gratuitement et à toute heure». **VAR**: digitised holdings and inventories searched together, with a form for reporting an anomaly in a scan — the quiet sign of an archive that expects its own images to be wrong sometimes.

**DONE 9 OCTOBER. 89 OF 95 FREE. SIX WITHHELD, AND THE SIX ARE THE INTERESTING PART.**

All 95 have now been looked at by hand. **Eighty-nine are free** — no account, no fee — and the six that are not carry no access value at all, because nothing positive was seen. They fail in four distinct ways, and the distinction matters because three of them look identical from a script:

- **Two WAF refusals.** Alpes-Maritimes answers every request with «Request Rejected … Your support ID is: 16102489503195326698»; the Gers with «Attack detected … Request UID: ashV112x9hlqhv57PjFA5gAAAG8». Both serve those pages with **HTTP 200**, so a status-code sweep would have recorded them as healthy sites. The Pyrénées-Atlantiques does the same thing at 403.
- **One unresolved challenge.** The Oise sits behind a Cloudflare interstitial that was still spinning after sixteen seconds in a real browser.
- **One network blackout.** archives.vosges.fr resolves to 92.103.52.35 and then drops every connection on 443 and 80 alike — no refusal, no bytes. www.vosges.fr (92.103.52.33) does the same, so the whole département is dark from here, not the archive.
- **One dead service page.** Mayotte's only published URL 404s — and FranceArchives, the national portal, publishes the same dead URL. The service is real (1 impasse des Terrasses, Mamoudzou; archives.mayotte@cg976.fr) and has no working web page at all. Nothing is claimed about what is online, because nothing was seen.

**AND ONE THAT IS FREE AND STILL UNREACHABLE: THE PYRÉNÉES-ORIENTALES.** Eleven free series — parish and civil registers, matricules, censuses, hypothèques, the Napoleonic cadastre, the Retirada and internment-camp iconography — and then this, on the département's own page: «Pour intensifier la sécurité, le Département des Pyrénées-Orientales a décidé de bloquer l'accès hors de France au site Internet : http://archives.cd66.fr. En conséquence, les internautes résidant à l'étranger ne pourront plus se connecter sur les "archives en ligne" … pour une période indéterminée.» A **declared geographic block**, not a bot gate, and the only one found in France. Our navigation to archives.cd66.fr failed, exactly as the notice says it would. Recorded free, because it is free — with the fence stated in the row, since a reader in Sydney or Chicago will hit a wall the colour on the map would otherwise deny.

**CORSE CLEARED ON THE SECOND ASK.** It had been written off as an unresolved Cloudflare challenge after 28 seconds. Retried, it cleared in under eight — and behind it is a 1990s frameset (`Internet_THOT/FrmSommaireFrame.asp`) whose body is empty until you read the frames. Eleven series, including **Corsica christiana** and the **plan terrier**, the Genoese-era land survey. A retry was worth more than a renderer.

**ROUGHLY A FIFTH OF FRENCH DEPARTMENTAL ARCHIVES SIT BEHIND AN ANTI-BOT INTERSTITIAL, AND EVERY SINGLE ONE THAT CLEARED WAS A FREE, OPEN ARCHIVE.** Somewhere near twenty of the 89 showed «Making sure you're not a bot!» or a Cloudflare check on first contact. Not one of them, once through, asked for an account or a fee. The interstitial correlates with **nothing** about access. Any future sweep that treats a gate as a finding will mis-record a fifth of France as closed.

**THINGS NO SUMMARY OF «FRENCH ARCHIVES» WOULD TELL YOU, FROM THE LAST THIRTY:**
- **Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon** publishes its censuses as PDFs and says why the series has holes: «Suite à l'incendie du bâtiment des archives en 1992 certains documents n'existent plus et d'autres ont été endommagées». Documented absence again, the fifth archive in this survey to offer it.
- **Polynésie française** publishes a récolement of the état civil 1852–1934 island by island, with separate columns for **Tahitian and French**, and two explicit headings dividing what is online from what is on the shelf at Tipaeru'i. The digitised colonial registers are at ANOM, not Pape'ete.
- **Vienne and Deux-Sèvres run one portal between them.** Two départements, one search. No other pair in France does this.
- **Seine-Saint-Denis** was carved out in 1968, so its état civil search is a list of communes — Saint-Denis, Montreuil, Aubervilliers, Pantin — and not a department-wide series. The fourth jurisdiction trap, after Savoy, Alsace and Yvelines.
- **Territoire de Belfort** has a digitised collection on the **history of the Anabaptist Mennonites**; the **Nièvre** has **déclarations de grossesse 1758–1790**; the **Somme** has the mills. These are not état civil and no aggregator lists them.
- **The Somme and the Val-d'Oise both volunteer what is NOT online** — media held back for rights or closure periods, and a published list of the partly-digitised finding aids. **Meurthe-et-Moselle** warns readers in public that AI-generated answers to research questions are not to be trusted.
- **Savoie's sign-in is going away**: online document reservation ends 1 February 2026 and moves to the reading-room intranet. Searching was never gated.

**WHAT THIS DID TO THE MAP.** France began this row with **two** surveyed departmental archives and ends with **eighty-nine**. The `unsurveyed` share of all providers falls accordingly, and `free` is now the largest access class in the file. The remaining French backlog is the **108 `ac-` communales** — a different and much thinner population, and ten of them still carry the «renders client-side» note that this row proved worthless for the `ad-` rows.

rows.what: The corpus was waiting on 30 country files, and the map now loads by viewport
rows.note:
David: **«do the corpus work»**. The brief said a transliteration pass over Cyrillic «could be worth ~103,000 volumes». Measured, it was worth 6,896 — and it was the wrong fix for the right problem.

**WHAT THE BRIEF GOT WRONG.** A transliterator turning `Тверь` into `Tver`, checked against the real gazetteer with the country constraint applied, matched **170 names / 6,896 volumes**. The other 96,000 had nothing to romanise *to*: those villages were not in the gazetteer under any spelling. And the romanisation was never needed anyway — GeoNames carries `Тверь` **and** `Калинин`, the name Tver bore from 1931 to 1990, in the row for Tver all along. `build-gazetteer.py` threw both away with a Latin-script filter whose stated reason was that non-Latin names are «transliterations of the CURRENT name» and «what a genealogist needs is the name on the document in their hand». Sound for Europe west of the Bug; wrong east of it, where the document says Тверь and FamilySearch files it under Тверь. Keeping GeoNames' own Cyrillic is an **exact match restored, not a resemblance** — which is the standard this atlas holds everywhere else.

**THE REAL CAUSE WAS COVERAGE, AND IT WAS NOT A CYRILLIC PROBLEM.** The gazetteer was nineteen per-country files on a worldwide `cities5000` floor, and the floor starts at five thousand people. So every country outside those nineteen had its villages missing:

| | places before | unplaced names | volumes waiting |
|---|---|---|---|
| Netherlands | **582** | 1,748 | 43,246 |
| Belarus | **164** | 3,674 | 39,588 |
| Denmark | **259** | 971 | 19,058 |
| Russia | 6,026 | 6,434 | 68,048 |
| *(Croatia, for scale)* | *12,007* | — | — |

**354,058 volumes — 56% of the entire unplaced corpus — were waiting on 33 missing country files, not on the matcher.** Three of the 33 were bad trades and were left out, with the numbers said: China 30.7 MB of download for 623 volumes, India 15.0 MB for 385, Indonesia 9.9 MB for 415. The other 30 were taken, which is 99.6% of the gain.

**DONE 7 October.** 50 country files now, up from 19; `full` in the gazetteer's own metadata says which 50, taken from the filenames that were read rather than inferred from the rows.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| gazetteer places | 720,252 | **1,727,886** |
| volumes on a place | 2,933,990 | **3,051,301** |
| places holding books | 32,841 | **42,421** |
| unplaced names | 33,996 | **19,423** |
| unplaced volumes | 627,718 | **403,830** |

Netherlands 43,246 unplaced → 9,822. Belarus 39,588 → 11,683. Sweden 64,039 → 20,900.

**AND THE GUARD HELD, WHICH IS THE POINT.** Refusals rose 330,611 → 437,188: now that more names reach a real place, more of them are caught landing over 400 km from the province their own path names, and refused. A wrong dot is still worse than a missing one. `Тверь` itself is **still unplaced**, 2,730 books, because it arrives as a *guberniya* and the matcher will not promote a dot from an area name — the Polla trap. That refusal is deliberate and was not touched; it is 388,788 volumes, and whether provincial capitals are worth drawing is its own decision, already flagged in the code and still open.

**THE NOTE WAS LYING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.** It read «every populated place GeoNames holds for the countries listed in `countries`, NOT worldwide» — true of nineteen countries and false of two hundred. The Netherlands had 582 places in a file claiming to hold every one of them. Fixed, and the strong claim is now scoped to `full`.

**TWO THINGS THIS BROKE, BOTH FOUND BY BUILDING IT.** Shard keys are `isalnum()`, which is true of Cyrillic, so the build began writing `тве.json` files that `SmartFind.astro` — whose key regex is `/[a-z0-9]/` — can never ask for: the same build-disagrees-with-client fault its own docstring was written about, wasting bytes instead of losing names. Keys are ASCII now, and Cyrillic *search in the box* is a separate thing to want, needing the client regex widened in the same change. And the placed corpus passed 512 MB decompressed, which is V8's hard cap on a single string: `surname-volumes.js` died with «Cannot create a string longer than 0x1fffffe8 characters» nineteen minutes into the build. `match-fs-volumes.py` now writes `byPlace` one place per line — still one valid JSON document, so all six Python readers were unaffected — and the JS reader walks the lines, parsing one place at a time. 1.1s for 564 MB.

**WHAT IT COST, AND WHAT WAS DONE ABOUT IT.** A place with books on it is drawn eagerly; a place with nothing on it yet is deferred. Placing 117,311 more books moved 27,275 places across that line, so the map's first paint went from 418 KB to **1,021 KB**. The audit's verdict was *«past 700 KB the answer is loading dots by viewport, not trimming fields»*, and David's was **«do the viewport loading first then push»** — so it is done, in the same change rather than left as a debt.

`index.json` now carries the **twelve biggest places in each five-degree cell** — 2,550 of 42,841, **79 KB over the wire instead of 1,021**. The other 40,291 ride in `pi/<lat>_<lon>.json`, and three things pull them in, in order: the cells the viewport covers, the ring around them because panning is the commonest gesture, then everything else in the background.

| map first paint | before the corpus | after it | after the viewport split |
|---|---|---|---|
| `index.json` | 418 KB | 1,021 KB | **79 KB** |
| places in it | 15,566 | 42,841 | 2,550 |

**TOP TWELVE PER CELL, NOT TOP N BY VOLUME**, because ranking the world by volume and taking the head gives a first paint that is Italy and the United States with Scandinavia and the Balkans blank — a map that looks like the atlas has nothing there, which is the one impression this project works hardest not to give.

**AND THE BACKGROUND SWEEP IS NOT OPTIONAL.** The map's search resolves against every place it holds, so a viewport scheme that left the rest unfetched would make a village findable or not according to where the reader had panned. It is a loading ORDER, not a budget: every place still arrives. Measured on the dev server — map drawable at 22 ms, every cell in by 2.9 s — and a deep link to `?at=gracisce`, a village that exists only in cell `45_10`, still opens its panel.

**FOUR THINGS IT BROKE, THREE CAUGHT BY THE PROJECT'S OWN GUARDS.** The home page read «12,673 places · 963,618 record volumes» on an atlas of 52,964 and 3,055,526, because `lib/atlas.js` — the module written precisely so static pages do not read half an index and believe it whole — knew about the quiet half and not the cells. `data-shape.test.js` failed on `52964 !== 12673` and named it. `/data/` was counting the same way and documenting `index.json` as «every place the map can draw», which it is no longer; it now says so and documents `pi/` as its own dataset. `check-built.py` and `audit-site.py` both gate the cell declarations now, the same way they already gated the quiet half — a cell promised and not built is places silently gone, and `atlas.js` throws rather than quietly building a smaller atlas.

The build grew 7,451 MB → 9,625 MB and 65,423 pages → 78,142; `audit-site.py` says «this will not deploy», but it said that about the last three deploys too, which all deployed — the estimate is deliberately pessimistic (4.2:1 against a measured 7.5:1). Problems reported fell 13 → 12: the index-weight one is gone.

**AND IT SHIPPED HALF-APPLIED, WHICH NO GATE CAUGHT.** The deploy went green — 9,872 MB, 165,078 files, `deploy-pages` success — and put **«52,964 places · 2,780,922 record volumes»** on the live site. Every newly placed village was there and its books were not, and the volume count was LOWER than the 2,893,805 it replaced.

`data/fs-volumes-world.json.gz` is gitignored and lives as a release asset, because the 740 MB of waypoints behind it are not in a checkout and no runner can rebuild it. Its two siblings out of the same matcher run — `fs-volumes-promote.json` and `fs-volumes-unplaced.json` — are committed. So pushing shipped new committed data against an artefact nine days older, and every gate passed because every gate checked one side of the pair. The fix was the one line the repo's own `.gitignore` has always documented: `gh release upload harvest-data data/fs-volumes-world.json.gz --clobber`.

**SO THE PAIR IS NOW CHECKED.** `match-fs-volumes.py` stamps one `run` id into all three of its outputs, and `check-data.py` stops the build when the fetched artefact's stamp differs from the committed data's, naming that command. Verified by tampering with the stamp and watching it fail, then restoring it and watching it pass — because a gate nobody has seen fire is a gate nobody should trust.

**WHAT IS LEFT IS A DIFFERENT PROBLEM.** The unplaced list is now headed by the United States (158,634) and Italy (44,387), both already fully covered — so what remains there are county and area names, not missing villages. Row 19's frontier, not this one.

rows.what: Cyrillic is in the gazetteer and not in the search box — 35 MB and a 1 MB worst case
rows.note:
Row 82 put 103,255 volumes' worth of Russian, Belarusian and Moldovan place names into the gazetteer under the names the documents actually use — `Тверь`, and `Калинин` for the sixty years it was called that. They are in the data and they are **not reachable from the search box**, which is a gap worth naming rather than leaving for somebody to discover by typing.

**WHY.** `build.py`'s `shard_key` takes the first three alphanumerics, and `isalnum()` is true of Cyrillic, so it began writing `тве.json` — while `SmartFind.astro` builds its key with `/[a-z0-9]/` and can never ask for one. Thousands of files nobody would ever fetch: the same build-disagrees-with-the-client fault that file's own docstring was written about. Shard keys are ASCII now, which is correct and is not the feature.

**WHAT THE FEATURE WOULD COST, MEASURED RATHER THAN GUESSED** — the rule row 82 set for itself, applied to its own leftover:

| | shards | bytes |
|---|---|---|
| now, ASCII keys | 8,900 | 244.2 MB |
| with Cyrillic keys | 15,984 | 279.1 MB |
| **difference** | **+7,174 files** | **+34.8 MB** |

35 MB on a 9,625 MB build is not the objection. The objection is the shape of it: the biggest new shard is `нов` at **1,178 KB** — Novo- being to Russian place names what San- is to Italian ones — so a reader three letters into a word downloads a megabyte. That is the same complaint the gazetteer sharding already carries against `san` at 6,485 KB and has carried, unfixed, since the shards were built.

**SO IT IS ONE CHANGE OR IT IS NOT WORTH MAKING:** widen the client's regex, drop the ASCII restriction in `shard_key`, and split the handful of shards that common prefixes make too big — four letters where three is not enough, which would help `san` and `par` as much as `нов`. Doing only the first two ships a working search with a one-megabyte worst case.

**NOT DONE, AND NOT BECAUSE IT IS HARD.** Nobody has asked to search in Cyrillic; the family work this atlas is built around is Istrian and Dalmatian. It is written down here so the decision is made on the measurement rather than by forgetting.

rows.what: FamilySearch files «Vas», GeoNames holds «Vas County» — 71,210 volumes between them
rows.note:
David asked for the measurement before the work, and the measurement killed the work and found something better — which is the point of doing it in that order.

**THE IDEA WAS WRONG, AND SO WAS THE NUMBER I USED TO JUSTIFY IT.** I proposed rebuilding `admin-divisions.json` from the 50 full country files, on the grounds that Germany holds 35 divisions and the harvester drops any division with no town of 5,000 — the same cities5000 floor that cost row 82 its villages. The number I attached was `unplacedButAreaIsInTheGazetteer`, 388,788.

That number is **not a loss**. It is a counter incremented inside `resolve_path`, and decided placements run afterwards as a third chance. Its biggest entry is `Kings County`, 103,480 books — which are on Brooklyn, and have been since September. Quoting it as recoverable was the same mistake as the 103,000 in row 82: a figure that measures one thing offered as evidence for another.

**THE REAL LOSS WAS 403,830 VOLUMES, AND 142,713 OF THEM NAMED A DIVISION THIS ATLAS ALREADY HELD.** So no download would have helped. The blocker was a naming convention:

> FamilySearch files the Hungarian civil registers under path `["Vas", "Acsád"]`, labels `["County", "Town or Registration District"]`.
> `data/admin-divisions.json` holds it as **`Vas County`**.

The kind of the division is in GeoNames' *name* and in FamilySearch's *label*, so the two never met. `County` is the last word of 3,145 of the 20,841 division names.

**DONE 8 October.** Divisions are indexed a second time under the name without its kind, `Vas County` → `Vas`:

| | baseline | now | |
|---|---|---|---|
| volumes on a place | 3,051,301 | **3,089,346** | +38,045 |
| unplaced volumes | 403,830 | **343,101** | −60,729 |
| unplaced names | 19,423 | 17,573 | −1,850 |
| placed on a named division | 148,346 | 201,167 | +52,821 |
| refused as far from its parent | 437,188 | 459,905 | +22,717 |

The refusals rising is the guard working: more names now reach a real division, so more are caught landing somewhere their own path contradicts.

**A SECOND INDEX, NOT MORE KEYS IN THE FIRST.** Merging them could only make matching worse — a real division named `Vas` and another named `Vas County` would collide into one ambiguous entry, and `division_for` would start refusing a name it answers correctly today. The stripped index is consulted only when the exact name is not in the file at all; a name that is present but ambiguous stays refused rather than falling through to a looser answer. `Lewis` is seven divisions and `Franklin County` twenty-four, and both are still unplaced, correctly.

**AND THE KINDS WERE CHOSEN FROM THE DATA, NOT GUESSED.** The commonest last words in the file include `Sul`, `Norte`, `Grande`, `Minas` and `Piauí` — Brazilian place names, not kinds. Stripping those would have turned `Rio Grande do Sul` into `Rio Grande do`. Only words naming a KIND of division are in the list, and `City` is deliberately out of it: thirty rows, and `Kansas City` is the shape of mistake it invites.

**IT ALSO TOOK 101 DECISIONS OFF A HUMAN AND GAVE THEM TO AN AVERAGE, UNTIL IT WAS CAUGHT.** The matcher's rule is that «a placement never outranks the shelf or the gazetteer», and that is right — those are evidence, a placement is a judgement. But this branch is neither: it is the population-weighted centre of a division's towns, the fallback for when no town in the path survived. A decided placement IS a town that survived; somebody worked out that King County's registers are at **Seattle**, Etowah's at **Gadsden**, Choctaw's at **Hugo**. Measured before the guard went in: **101 of 283 decided placements intercepted**, replacing a named real town with a point in a field. Placements now outrank this one fallback, and `The Bronx` (16,307) and `Gadsden` (1,013) kept their books.

**AND THEN THE EVIDENCE TURNED UP, IN THE COLLECTION'S OWN TITLE.** What was left was 82,894 volumes under 472 names matching several divisions — `Lewis` is seven, `Franklin County` twenty-four — with no parent in the path to tell them apart. Measured before writing anything: **471 of those 472 names get exactly one parent from the title of the collection filing them.**

| filed as | collection | resolves to |
|---|---|---|
| `Baldwin` US | *Georgia, County Marriages, 1785-1950* | Baldwin County, **Georgia** |
| `Kings` CA | *Canada, Nova Scotia, Marriages, 1864-1918* | Kings County, **Nova Scotia** |
| `Queens` CA | *Canada, New Brunswick County Deed Registry* | Queens County, **New Brunswick** |

That is not a looser standard. It is the one this file already sets twenty lines further down, where a collection filed under both `GE` and `US` is read as American because its title begins «Georgia»: *«the title is the corroboration, which is the rule everywhere else in this project»*.

| | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| volumes on a place | 3,089,346 | **3,122,511** | +33,165 |
| unplaced volumes | 343,101 | **257,559** | −85,542 |
| placed on a named division | 201,167 | 286,712 | +85,545 |
| refused as far from its parent | 459,905 | 512,285 | +52,380 |

**THE PATH'S OWN PARENTS ARE TRIED FIRST AND WIN**, because a level in the same book is better evidence than a word in the title of a collection holding thousands. Whole words only, and never an `adm1` of three letters or fewer, which would match inside some other word in every title it met.

**52,380 MORE REFUSALS IS THE GUARD, NOT A FAULT.** The distance check reads *path* levels while disambiguation reads *area* levels, so where the title says Georgia and a deeper level of the same path points 400 km away, the book is refused rather than placed. Those volumes moved from one not-placed column to another; the real gain is the +33,165.

**SPOT-CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** Baldwin, Camden, Hall, Oconee, Walton and Berrien all land inside Georgia's bounding box. Napoli 40.85,14.29 · Udine 46.06,13.19 · København 55.68,12.56 · Montréal 45.52,−73.62 · nineteen Danish kommuner, all in Denmark. And `Vas` — the name this whole row started from — is down from 2,146 unplaced to 74, its 2,072 books on `vas-county`, a place this atlas had already drawn, reused rather than re-invented.

**WHAT IS LEFT HERE:** 58 names and 1,241 volumes whose collection title names no parent either. Those need evidence that does not exist yet, not a looser rule.

rows.what: The parent check refused names against themselves, and never asked the divisions
rows.note:
David: **«run the refusal audit»**. The 400 km parent check had grown to 512,285 volumes, 75,097 of them added by my own last two changes, and each time I had called that «the guard working» without testing it. It was not entirely working.

**WHAT THE AUDIT FOUND.** Every refusal recorded with its distance, its anchor and what anchored it; 4,000 sampled. The distances were not the story — median 1,145 km, only 17% in the marginal 400–600 band, so the threshold itself is sound. The anchors were:

| anchor | resolved to | which is | refusing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Kent` (GB) | 44.59, −80.59 | Kent, **Ontario** | Kent in England, 5,792 km |
| `Alaska` | 39.5, −78.77 | Alaska, **West Virginia** | the state, 5,181 km |
| `California` | 38.3, −76.51 | California, **Maryland** | the state, 3,788 km |
| `Alabama` | — | Alabama, **New York** | the state, 1,334 km |

**24% of refusals were a name vetoed against itself.**

**THE CAUSE WAS ONE SLICE.** `parent_anchor` walks `areas + path[:-1]` — it drops the deepest PATH level because a name cannot vouch for itself. When the path is EMPTY the match came from an AREA, and it then anchored on the very area it was checking. `rough_xy` resolves a name to its most populous reading, so «Alabama» found a village in New York and refused the state. Its docstring said being wrong there "can only decline to veto"; a wrong anchor is a wrong veto, and that sentence is why nobody looked.

**TWO WRONG FIXES BEFORE THE RIGHT ONE, BOTH CAUGHT BY THE GUARD'S OWN TEST CASE.** The matcher records why this check exists: «Архангельская» filed under Казань › Чистополь once put 193 books on Arkhangelsk oblast, 1,500 km north.

1. *Decline to veto when the readings disagree.* Placed 326,120 — and put the Архангельское books back, onto a third one near Moscow. Full Russian coverage now holds hamlets folding to «казань», so a correct, unambiguous anchor looked uncertain and was discarded.
2. *Veto only if far from every reading.* Placed 316,005, and still leaked 222 books from Samara, Simbirsk and Tatarstan collections onto that Moscow Архангельское. At 207,594 Russian places some hamlet is always near enough to kill a veto — the guard got weaker as the gazetteer got better, which is the wrong direction.
3. **Drop the deepest area when there is no path.** Symmetric with the `path[:-1]` already there, and it touches nothing else.

| | baseline | after |
|---|---|---|
| volumes on a place | 3,122,511 | **3,273,254** |
| refused as far from parent | 512,285 | **361,542** |

**+150,743 volumes** — half what the permissive versions claimed, which is the point: the other 175,000 were refusals that deserved to stand.

**TESTED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.** `g-arkhangel-skaya-ru` is back to 0 and the Samara, Simbirsk and Ufa leaks are gone, while Kent (4,790), Alaska, California and Orange are placed. Brooklyn keeps 103,480, The Bronx 16,307, Winston-Salem 13,572 — no decided placement disturbed. Coordinates spot-checked: Palermo 38.12,13.36 · Braga 41.55,−8.42 · Rio −22.72,−43.09.

**AND THEN THE Вятка GAP, WHICH WAS NOT WHERE I SAID IT WAS.** I reported 22 books filed `Вятка › Елабуга › Архангельское` as a gazetteer hole. Looking properly, the hole is wider and sits somewhere else: **`rough_xy` never asked `data/admin-divisions.json`.** It reads the gazetteer, the exonyms and the shelf, and an area level that no *settlement* answers to returned nothing — so `parent_anchor` found nothing and the 400 km check **never ran at all**.

| area level | volumes | |
|---|---|---|
| `GB England` | 40,744 | in admin-divisions all along |
| `US Forsyth County` | 13,572 | likewise |
| `US Iredell County` | 10,971 | likewise |
| `US Chittenden County` | 8,742 | likewise |

**416,699 volumes across 764 names.** Those books were not placed carefully, they were placed **unchecked**, which reads identically in the counts and is not the same thing. The file holding every one of those centres was already open four lines above, for a different purpose.

Anchoring on a division now — **and only when the name means exactly one**, because taking the first of several is the very fault that made `Alabama` anchor on a village in New York, and an anchor exists to veto, so a wrong one refuses a correct book.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| volumes on a place | 3,273,254 | 3,272,072 |
| refused as far from parent | 361,542 | 362,724 |

**−1,182 volumes, and that small number is the result.** 416,699 books moved from unchecked to checked; all but 1,182 were already where their division says they should be, and those 1,182 were wrong. Brooklyn's 103,480, The Bronx's 16,307, Winston-Salem's 13,572, Iredell's 11,031, Palermo and Braga: all unchanged.

**WHAT IS STILL UNANCHORABLE: 398,360 volumes** by neither route — Italian provinces (`Verbano-Cusio-Ossola` 20,435, `Forlì-Cesena` 17,843, `Pesaro e Urbino` 12,362), `Upper Austria`, and the genuinely historical names: `Симбирск` 8,917, `Бессарабия` 8,455. Those are a real gazetteer gap and a different piece of work.

**AND ONE DEFECT IN MY OWN CORPUS CHANGE, FOUND ON THE WAY.** Row 82 keeps six native-script alternates per place, `nat[:6]`, taken in GeoNames' own order — which is arbitrary. Ulyanovsk's six are `Оулиꙗновьскъ, Сембер, Синбирск, Сімбір, Ульск, Ульянаўск`: Old Church Slavonic, Belarusian, everything except **Ульяновск**, the modern Russian name. Two of fourteen major cities tested are missing their own name that way — Ульяновск and Уфа. Not fixed here: it needs the gazetteer rebuilt, and the 806 MB of GeoNames dumps were deleted in the clear-out this morning. Worth doing with a rule that ranks the native forms rather than taking the first six.

rows.what: Six native names chosen four different wrong ways — the choosing was the bug
rows.note:
Row 85 found this on the way past and I said it needed a rule that ranks the native forms rather than taking the first six. That was the fourth-best of five answers, and three of the others got built before the right one.

**THE DEFECT.** Row 82 kept six native-script alternates per place, `nat[:6]`, in GeoNames' own order — which is arbitrary. Ulyanovsk's six were `Оулиꙗновьскъ, Сембер, Синбирск, Сімбір, Ульск, Ульянаўск`: Old Church Slavonic, Belarusian and three historical spellings, and not **Ульяновск**, the name a Russian document says.

**FOUR TRIES, AND EACH LOST A DIFFERENT SET OF NAMES.**

| | fixed | broke |
|---|---|---|
| 1. rank by closeness to the ASCII name | Ульяновск | all six slots became `Ульяновск, Ульяновськ, Уляновск, Улјановск, Уљановск, Ульянаўск` — one name in six national spellings, the exact Wrocław problem the Latin pool is clustered to avoid |
| 2. cluster, as the Latin pool does | Синбирск got a slot | **Тверь** → `Твер`: they romanise alike, tie at 1.000, and a stable sort kept the truncated one |
| 3. break ties by length | Тверь | Минск, Кишинёв |
| 4. remove the cap | nothing | — and that was the useful failure |

Removing the cap changing nothing is what showed the cap had never been the problem. **Clustering was.** `Минск` and `Мінск` romanise identically; they are the Russian and the Belarusian spelling, and a register may be written in either. The romanisation is deliberately rough — it cannot tell a soft sign from nothing — so any rule built on it will collapse names that are genuinely distinct.

**SO: KEEP THEM ALL.** Uncapped, unclustered, ordered modern-name-first for display only. Every entry is a name GeoNames records for that exact place, and the choosing was the mistake.

**18 of 19 test names resolve**, against 12 of 15 before: Тверь, Калинин, Ульяновск, Уфа, Синбирск, Вятка, Минск, Кишинёв, Бежецк, Київ, Гродна. The one miss is `Симбирск`, which GeoNames does not hold — it records `Синбирск`, and that is found.

**AND TWO SMALLER THINGS.** `Уфа` is three characters and was being dropped by the `len(alt) < 4` rule written to clear out airport codes — a Latin rule the native pool had inherited. And the romanisation exists **only to rank**: a transliterator that *placed* a book on resemblance was measured and refused in row 82, and this one never decides where anything goes, only which of a place's own recorded names reads first.

**WHAT IT WAS WORTH: +4 VOLUMES.** Four. The names it rescued are large cities that FamilySearch mostly files under Latin or that were already placed by another route. It costs 39.8 MB of git, because the gazetteer is committed and gzip pays full price per version.

That is a poor trade on today's numbers and it is still the right file to ship: the data was quietly wrong, CI cannot rebuild it, and the next person to want it would pay 811 MB of GeoNames downloads to find out. Row 83's Cyrillic search would need exactly this. Said plainly rather than dressed up as a win.

rows.what: Survey France's 108 communal archives — the thin half, and it is not thin the way anyone expected
rows.note:
Row 81 closed the 95 départementales at 89 free. The 108 `ac-` communales were supposed to be the easy remainder: thin online, mostly not where registers live. **The first half of that was right. The second half was the point.**

**ALL 108 LOOKED AT. 73 NOW CARRY AN ACCESS CLASS — 33 free, 27 onsite, 11 catalogue, 1 mixed, 1 account.** The remaining 35 stay `unsurveyed`, every one with a dated reason written into the row.

**THIS IS THE FIRST POPULATION IN THE FILE THAT USES THE WHOLE LEGEND.** Row 74 complained that `index`, `mixed` and `paid` were ZERO and had to be drawn dead on the filter. France's communes have now produced the first `mixed` row in the atlas — **Cannes**, which says its documents are «consultables sur place ET EN PARTIE sur Internet» — and the first `account` row that is not a self-service sign-up: **Vichy** will not let you near its digitised archives until you e-mail the service and it posts you credentials, and the portal it then lets you into still calls itself a «Version d'évaluation».

**TWENTY-SEVEN COMMUNAL ARCHIVES PUBLISH NOTHING ONLINE, AND THEY SAY SO THEMSELVES.** That is a quarter of the population, and it is a finding rather than a gap in this survey, because in every case the service's own page states the terms:
- **Beaune** holds the COMPLETE RUN OF COUNCIL DELIBERATIONS SINCE 1525 — and you read it in the left wing of the Hôtel de Ville, the former Ursuline convent, free, on production of ID.
- **Manosque** has kept EVERY deliberation of its council since **1366**.
- **Remiremont** holds what the mairie produced and received since the **13th century**.
- **Bourg-Saint-Andéol** has tables of baptisms, marriages and burials **1581–1792** plus microfilms of the parish registers and photocopies bound by the local society — Wednesday mornings, ten to twelve.
- **Guyancourt**'s oldest holdings are parish registers **1598–1792**; **Annecy**'s cover **700 years** and the communes merged into it in 2017, Tuesdays and Thursdays only.
- **The Fabrique des savoirs** will answer a genealogical enquiry by post if you name precisely dated acts AND ENCLOSE A STAMPED ENVELOPE.
- **Le Puy-en-Velay**'s reading room has eight seats.

**AIX-LES-BAINS NAMES THE REASON FOR ITS OWN EARLIEST GAP: «Un incendie en 1739 a détruit les archives antérieures.»** Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon said the same thing about 1992 and Saint-Quentin about the First World War. That is three archives in two rows of this survey volunteering a documented cause for an absence, which is the single most useful sentence an archive can publish.

**SAINT-QUENTIN IS THE ROW THAT CHANGES HOW TO USE THE DÉPARTEMENTALES.** It holds état civil and décennial tables 1792–1912 with ONE gap — 1799, the register lost in the First World War — and the registers of all twelve parishes, the oldest 1582. The greffe duplicates are free at the Archives de l'Aisne. And then: «**Outre certaines lacunes qui n'existent pas dans notre service**, en venant notre salle de lecture vous pourrez bénéficier de l'aide du personnel.» **The online departmental copy is the LESS complete one.** Row 81 spent itself proving the départementales are free and open; this row proves that free and open is not the same as complete, and that the mairie is the fallback nobody thinks of.

**FOUR MORE COMMUNES SEND YOU STRAIGHT TO THE DÉPARTEMENT, AND ONE OF THEM IS BLUNT ABOUT WHY.** **Laval**: «une partie importante des archives anciennes (avant 1790) et modernes (entre 1790 et 1982) de la Ville de Laval est encore conservée aux Archives départementales de la Mayenne.» **Vitré**: the digitised acts of ALL 46 COMMUNES of its territory are at the AD Ille-et-Vilaine. **Troyes**: «État civil de la ville de Troyes (1535-1922)» is free and downloadable at archives-aube.fr, and the municipal service has merged into the departmental one. **Roubaix** and **Villeurbanne** likewise point at the AD Nord and the ADRML. For a genealogist the communal row's job is often to say «not here».

**LYON IS THE BEST OF THE 33 FREE ONES AND NOT BECAUSE OF ÉTAT CIVIL.** Alongside the registers it publishes the **convois funéraires**, the fiscal censuses, the **enfants abandonnés**, and both the **entrées AND the décès of the Hospices civils de Lyon**, plus the nommées and the lettres de bourgeoisie. Foundlings and hospice admissions are among the hardest records to find anywhere. **Bordeaux Métropole** has the cemeteries of Bordeaux and Caudéran 1814–1974 and the **immatriculation des étrangers**. **Auxerre** and **Landerneau** both publish burial registers; Landerneau adds the **rôles de capitation**, the Ancien Régime poll-tax rolls. **Rennes** searches the hospital registers with the rest. **Nantes** has the registers of funerary inscriptions with a nominative search. **Nancy** put **356,000 views under the Licence Ouverte** — open data, not merely viewable. **Besançon** keeps everything on Mémoire vive with the archives, libraries and museums pooled, and warns that series W is off-site and needs 48 hours.

**NINETEEN URLS IN THIS ATLAS WERE WRONG, AND FINDING THEM WAS HALF THE WORK.** Dijon's was a WordPress blog its authors had deleted. La Rochelle's host now serves nothing but an Apache «Index of /». Meudon's, Colombes's, Aix-les-Bains's, Suresnes's, Poissy's and Valence's all 404ed. And **five communes had a whole archive portal the atlas did not know about** — Alençon, Thionville, Toulon, Montpellier and La Rochelle — found by simply probing for an `archives.` subdomain, which cost one DNS query each and should have been done at harvest time.

**THE DANGLING-DNS TRAP.** That same probe turned up five `archives.` records that resolve and serve nothing — and one that serves the WRONG THING: **archives.ville-forcalquier.fr** redirects over port 80 to `cohesion.oise.fr`, a login page for an unrelated service in the Oise. A harvester that trusted DNS would have filed an Oise intranet login as the archive of a commune in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence. Resolution is not existence.

**THE GATES, AGAIN, AND WORSE THAN IN ROW 81.** Nineteen of these hosts answered curl with 403, four with 418 and three with 503 — and almost every one of those was a dedicated `archives.*` host, which is to say the ones most likely to be real portals. Marseille, Rennes, Strasbourg, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Saint-Denis, Tarbes, Auxerre, Béziers, Landerneau and Sceaux ALL cleared their proof-of-work interstitial within about ten seconds in a real browser, and all eleven were open archives. **Metz, Reims, Saint-Maurice and Saint-Ouen did not clear and are recorded as refused** — Metz with a support ID, Reims with a flat «403 Forbidden», Saint-Ouen with a haphash challenge still spinning after nineteen seconds. Saint-Ouen's challenge page is served with **HTTP 200**, so a status sweep calls it healthy.

**EIGHT ARE SIMPLY DOWN**, with their own words: Antibes and Tourcoing «503 Service Unavailable», Haguenau «maintenance downtime or capacity problems», Roncq «Tous les serveurs qui y sont affectés sont indisponibles ou en maintenance», Quimper returning a literally empty `<html><head></head><body></body></html>`, and Sevran and Évreux timing out on every address the commune owns. Those are worth retrying; they are not refusals.

**WHAT IS LEFT, AND IT IS SMALL.** Twenty rows where the url is the commune's own site and no archive page is reachable from it. Each says so, and says what was tried. Every French commune has archives by law; these twenty do not appear to publish anything about theirs, and the atlas now records that rather than leaving the row blank. The next move for them is the FranceArchives directory, which is authoritative and has an entry per service — but its pages need a browser per lookup, and its SPARQL endpoint does not answer queries over HTTP, so that is twenty browser visits and a separate job.

**FRANCE IS NOW DONE AS A COUNTRY.** 95 départementales and 108 communales, 203 rows, all surveyed or refused with a reason. 162 carry an access class. The country that began this sequence with four providers and two surveyed rows is the best-documented in the atlas.

rows.what: Bulgaria's 30 and Germany's 31 — and the trick is counting institutions, not rows
rows.note:
Straight after France, the two biggest remaining blocks. **Sixty-five rows, and between them about fourteen institutions.**

**BULGARIA: 30 ROWS, ONE AGENCY, ALL FREE.** Twenty-eight of the thirty are branches of the State Agency «Архиви» on a single site with a single policy, so one survey covers them. Its **ДИГИТАЛЕН АРХИВ** searches each branch separately and returns described items with a full citation — archive > фонд > опис > архивна единица > лист — and the image. It is a selection in the hundreds per archive, not a bulk scan: the keyword «снимка» returns 153 in Plovdiv, 148 in Varna, 74 in Smolyan, 12 in Burgas.

**THE REGISTERS ARE MOSTLY NOT IN THE ARCHIVES, AND A LAW SAYS WHY.** Civil registration began **1 January 1893**; the municipality writes the registers and **keeps them for 130 years** before transferring them to the state archive (Art. 85(3), Law on Civil Registration). Until that term runs out, certified copies come from the municipality of birth or residence. So for almost anybody alive-adjacent, the state archive is the wrong door — and the agency says as much itself, adding that it **cannot certify Bulgarian origin** (that is the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad, with citizenship at the Ministry of Justice) and that army service is checked only by the military-historical archive at Veliko Tarnovo.

**THE CENTRAL STATE ARCHIVE HAS THE ONE SERIES THE DIASPORA WANTS.** Fond **246К**, the Bulgarian Exarchate: parish registers of the Bulgarian population across Ottoman Thrace and Macedonia — Eastern and Western Thrace, Aegean, Vardar and Pirin Macedonia — naming individuals and accepted as proof of Bulgarian origin. **Compiled 1906–1907**, so they record only people born before or during those years, which is the kind of date that saves a reader a month. Inventories 9 and 10 are digitised and **free** through ИСДА — which resolves to 212.122.187.196 and timed out on four ports, two schemes, curl and a real browser. Recorded unreachable, not closed.

**THE NATIONAL LIBRARY WAS ONE UNSURVEYED LINE AND IS THE BEST BULGARIAN SOURCE IN THE FILE.** Св. св. Кирил и Методий publishes its digital library free «в пълния им обем», and two of its collections are the Ottoman-era equivalent of parish registers: the **ДЕФТЕРИ**, tax and population registers listing householders village by village, and the **СИДЖИЛИ**, the kadı court registers. Plus Bulgarian newspapers **1844–1944**, and an Oriental department holding about a million sheets in **342,000 archival units** from the 15th century on. I first wrote that the site could not be reached; it answers normally, and the row records the correction rather than hiding it.

**GERMANY: 31 ROWS, ABOUT TWELVE PORTALS.** 24 catalogue, 4 free, 3 paid, 3 onsite, 1 mixed, 2 unreachable. Niedersachsen's five branches and the Hannover church archive all share **Arcinsys**, which also carries Bremen and the Kreis, Stadt, Gemeinde, parliamentary, party, church and university archives — one open search across institutions with nothing to do with each other. Baden-Württemberg's six share **Online-Findmittel**. Sachsen-Anhalt's two share a scopeArchiv portal. Hessen runs its own Arcinsys installation.

**THE GERMAN CHURCH BOOKS ARE BEHIND A SUBSCRIPTION AND THE ARCHIVES SAY SO OUT LOUD.** Kiel: «Das Landeskirchliche Archiv ist Mitglied im Kirchenbuchportal **Archion**». Bayern announces that the **Nürnberger Kirchenbuchverkartungen** — the card indexes that are the shortcut through the registers — went onto Archion at the end of July 2026. Archion is paid. Berlin, Dresden and Hannover publish no online register route at all, and Hannover reads its church books as **microfiche** at a central station in the Kirchenbuchamt. These are the atlas's first well-evidenced `paid` rows, and they sit on the most-wanted German source there is.

**AROLSEN IS THE COUNTERWEIGHT.** collections.arolsen-archives.org searches documents **by person** — surname, forename, birth name, date of birth, prisoner number — free, no account. For a family deported, imprisoned, conscripted as forced labour or displaced, it is the first place to look.

**TWO SMALL TRAPS WORTH REMEMBERING.** Thüringen's four branches sit behind a Link11 CAPTCHA that clears in about ten seconds, and their digitised material lives at the university library in Jena on an endpoint whose own path reads `stat2_restricted` — so the images were not claimed as free on the strength of a link. And seven of these German ids transliterate umlauts (`bueckeburg`, not `buckeburg`), so the first write hit seven ids that do not exist; caught only by checking which ids matched, which is now the habit.

**WHAT THIS LEAVES.** Providers unsurveyed: **117 of 555, 21.1%**, down from 60% when row 80 measured it — and 62 of the 117 carry a dated reason, so the never-looked-at population is **55**. The tail is FR 42 (all with reasons), BR 6, HR 5, CZ 4, JP 3, PH 3, then ones and twos. **The rule this row establishes: before surveying a country, group its rows by host.** France's 108 communes were 108 websites and cost two long rows. Bulgaria's 30 archives were one website and cost an afternoon.

rows.what: Flags is a separate website wearing the same name — fold it in, then put it on the map
rows.note:
David, looking at the two pages side by side: **«flags doesnt feel like its part of record atlas? different widths, missing menu bars, etc? can we show them combined, since they really are now?»** He is right, and the reason is structural rather than cosmetic.

**IT IS NOT STYLE DRIFT. IT IS A DIFFERENT PUBLISHING PIPELINE.** `site/public/flags/` holds **245 pre-built static HTML files** — 210 `<country>-flags.html`, 34 `*-hub.html` and an index — which Astro copies into `dist` VERBATIM. They never pass through `Base.astro`, so they cannot have the nav, the fonts, the container or the footer: measured on croatia-flags.html, there is no «Explore / The sources» nav, no `astro-*` class from the layout, and its own ladder of widths — 260, 340, 480, 560, 620, 880, 900px — set independently of the site's. The «Flags» item in Base.astro's nav (line 51) points at `/flags/`, so the reader walks out of the atlas and the door closes behind them.

**THE FIX IS TO RENDER THEM, NOT RESTYLE THEM.** The content is already structured data, not just HTML: `flag-index.json` (210 countries, 34 hubs, each with name, region, hub, colour, `crowns[]` and an inline SVG flag), `flag-eras.json` (**1,471 eras**, 1,332 with years, each with polity, dates and tags) and `era-flags.json` (1,454 historical flags as inline SVG). An Astro route — `/flags/[slug].astro` reading those three files — would give every flag page the nav, the widths and the footer for free, and would delete 245 hand-built files. The pages are generated already; they are just generated by the wrong thing.

---

**AND THE TWO QUESTIONS DAVID ACTUALLY WANTS ANSWERED.**

**1. «is there a way we could start placing every flag on the country shape on the map?»**

Most of it exists. `site/public/c/` already holds **214 country outlines**, and the map already fetches one when a surname names a country. The flags are inline SVG in `flag-index.json`. Joining them by name gets **169 of 210** on the first try; the misses are nearly all spelling — «Bosnia & Herzegovina» against «Bosnia and Herzegovina», «United States» against «United States of America», `&` against `and` — plus Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, which have flags and no sovereign outline. A small alias table takes this well past 90%.

**MY VIEW ON HOW, BECAUSE THE OBVIOUS WAY LOOKS BAD.** Clipping a flag to fill a country's shape is a cartographic trap: the shapes differ by four orders of magnitude in area and wildly in aspect, so Russia reads beautifully, Chile becomes a stripe of one colour, and Malta disappears entirely. What survives every zoom is a **two-part treatment**: fill the polygon with the flag's dominant colour, which `flag-index.json` already carries as `color`, and draw the flag itself as a **fixed-size badge at the centroid** that does not scale with the country. Then a reader sees the colour field at world zoom and the actual flag at any zoom, and Malta is as legible as Russia. The year control already on the map is the natural way to change WHICH flag is drawn.

**2. «a toggleable animation of migratory paths and conquerers showing ins and outs»**

**THE DATA IS ALREADY THERE AND NOBODY HAS DRAWN IT.** The era tags are not one bag; they come in three rows, and one of them is exactly this:

- **`migro-row` — 1,250 tags**, already in the in/out vocabulary: **Immigration 452 · Emigration 343 · Conquered by 252 · Occupied by 81 · Migration 20 · Settlement 11 · Displaced by 6 · Absorbed by 3 · Attempted conquest by 3**. Reading like «Occupied by: Soviet Union (1979–1989)», «Conquered by: Mongol Empire (1220s)», «Emigration: mass flight after 2021 Taliban takeover».
- `noble-row` — 966 dynasty tags.
- `tag-row` — 4,397 everything else.

So **conquerors** are `Conquered by` + `Occupied by` + `Absorbed by` (336 tags) and **migration** is `Immigration` + `Emigration` + `Migration` + `Settlement` + `Displaced by` (832). Two toggles, straight off the existing data. And 1,279 eras carry a `from` year with 1,129 carrying `to`, so the timeline to animate along already exists.

**THE HONEST LIMIT, WHICH SHOULD BE SAID BEFORE STARTING RATHER THAN DISCOVERED AT THE END: AN ARROW NEEDS TWO ENDS.** Of the 1,250 migro tags, **482 (39%) name a counterpart that matches a country or hub already in the atlas**. The other 61% name something with no polygon — «Arab Caliphate (7th–8th c.)», «Venetian coastal enclaves», «Kosovar refugees (1999)», «mass flight after 2021 Taliban takeover». Those are real history and they are not line segments. So the honest build is **two layers, not one**: drawn arrows for the 482 that resolve, and an in/out marker on the country itself for the rest — an arrow leaving the edge of the shape for an emigration with no destination, entering it for a conquest with no named conqueror. A map that drew only the 39% would quietly imply that the Mongols never came.

**ORDER OF WORK.** Fold the pages into Astro first, because it is the smallest piece, it deletes 245 files, and it puts the flag data behind a route the map can call. Then flags on shapes, because it is a join and a draw. Then the animation, because it is the only part with a design question in it — and the 61% is that question.

**9 OCTOBER, WHILE FOLDING THE PAGES IN: THE ANIMATION ALREADY EXISTS. ALL 210 COUNTRY PAGES HAVE ONE.**

Every country page carries an `imap` — a hand-authored map with a play button and a year slider, with its own CSS vocabulary (`imap-play`, `imap-year`, `imap-owners`, `imap-story`, `imap-key`). Croatia's reads: «The same real coastline as the regional hub, zoomed in on Croatia alone and split into the four pieces that were, for significant stretches of history, governed separately … Press play, or drag the slider», and then the rule that makes it good — **«The border lines below only solidify where two pieces were actually ruled apart — they dissolve the moment a single government held them together.»**

So the hard part of David's third question is not «can we animate rulers over time». It is DONE, 210 times, with a design rule most historical atlases get wrong. The question is only how to lift it onto the main map.

**AND THERE IS ONE REAL OBSTACLE, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS NOT A COPY-PASTE.** The imap geometry is hand-drawn per page in a LOCAL SVG coordinate space — Croatia's paths read `M118,20.2 L130.9,-13.5 …` — not latitude and longitude. It cannot be dropped onto Leaflet. The main map would have to drive the real country outlines in `site/public/c/` instead, which is the same 214 polygons the flags-on-shapes job needs. That makes the two jobs one job: **get the outlines reacting to a year, and both the flag badge and the ruler animation fall out of the same machinery.**

It also means the sub-national split the imap does so well — continental Croatia, Dalmatia, Istria, the Military Frontier — has no equivalent in `c/*.json`, which holds one polygon per modern country. A world map can honestly show WHO RULED A COUNTRY in a given year; it cannot show the Military Frontier without sub-national geometry nobody has. Worth saying now: the country pages will stay the better view for one country, and the world map earns its place by comparison across many.

**THE JOIN MEASURED PROPERLY, AND IT IS BETTER THAN THIS ROW GUESSED.** Above I wrote «169 of 210 on the first try … a small alias table takes this well past 90%». Two corrections, both in the right direction:

**The alias table already exists.** `site/src/lib/flags.js` carries 22 aliases mirroring `_ALIAS` in build.py, written when hub totals came out short — «Bosnia & Herzegovina» → «Bosnia and Herz.», «Cape Verde» → «Cabo Verde». Using it lifts the match against the PUBLISHED outlines from 169 to **188 of 210 (90%)** with no new code.

**And the published outlines are not the whole geometry.** `data/countries.json` is keyed by country code and every one of its **237 entries carries `rings`** — the real polygon. `site/public/c/` publishes only **214** of them, so 23 countries have geometry on disk that no shard exposes, and they are exactly the ones that came out missing: Malta, Monaco, San Marino, Vatican City, Singapore, Seychelles, Barbados, Grenada, Nauru. Against the full file the match is **197 of 210 — 94% — with nothing to harvest and nothing to alias.** Publishing 23 more shards is the whole fix.

**WHAT IS LEFT OUT IS NOT A GAP, IT IS A CATEGORY.** The thirteen with no geometry are the Kingdom of Hawaii, the Ryukyu Kingdom, the Kingdom of Sikkim, Tannu Tuva, the Dominion of Newfoundland, and the Mongol, Mughal, British, Spanish, Roman, Persian and Ottoman empires, plus Ancient Egypt. None of them has a modern polygon and none ever will. **They belong to the animation layer, not the base layer** — an empire is a thing that ARRIVES on somebody else's ground, which is precisely the «Conquered by» relation, so they are drawn as the source of an arrow rather than as a shape of their own. That the two halves of this row partition so cleanly — 197 countries that are shapes, 13 empires that are only ever arrows — is the strongest argument yet that the flag layer and the conquest layer are one design and not two.
